reference.source: Standard haematopoietic cell transplantation and transplant immunology reference texts
clinicalPearls: Arises after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation when engrafted donor T lymphocytes recognise recipient tissues as foreign and mount an immune attack, classically within the first weeks to months
The three principal target organs are the skin, the gastrointestinal tract, and the liver
Skin disease typically begins as a maculopapular rash often involving the palms, soles, and ears, which can become confluent, bullous, or desquamating in severe cases
Gut involvement produces profuse, often secretory, watery diarrhoea with crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and anorexia, the last reflecting upper-gut disease
Liver involvement gives a cholestatic picture with rising bilirubin and cholestatic enzymes
Severity is described by staging each affected organ and combining these into an overall clinical grade that guides treatment intensity and predicts outcome
Risk rises with HLA mismatch, unrelated or older donors, older recipients, and reduced graft-versus-host prophylaxis
First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids added to baseline calcineurin-inhibitor-based immunosuppression, with steroid-refractory disease carrying a poor prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Conditioning-related tissue injury releases inflammatory cytokines and exposes host antigens, priming an immune response. Donor T lymphocytes contained within the graft recognise recipient major and minor histocompatibility antigens presented on host cells, become activated, and proliferate. This drives a cytokine-amplified inflammatory cascade in which activated donor effector cells attack epithelial targets in the skin, gut, and liver, producing the characteristic rash, diarrhoea, and cholestasis. The intensity of the response reflects the degree of donor-recipient mismatch and the adequacy of immunosuppressive prophylaxis.
additionalDifferentials: Drug eruption from conditioning agents or antimicrobials
Viral exanthem or systemic viral reactivation such as cytomegalovirus or human herpesvirus 6
Infective enterocolitis including Clostridioides difficile or cytomegalovirus colitis
Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome as an alternative cause of cholestasis and hyperbilirubinaemia
Cholestasis from drugs, parenteral nutrition, or sepsis
Engraftment syndrome in the peri-engraftment period
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm and characterise cutaneous involvement histologically
Endoscopy with mucosal biopsy of stomach, duodenum, or rectosigmoid for suspected gut disease
Liver function tests to define the cholestatic pattern, with liver biopsy reserved for uncertain cases
Stool studies and viral testing to exclude infective enterocolitis
Blood viral PCR for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and adenovirus given the immunosuppressed state
Assessment of donor engraftment and chimerism
Clinical and imaging assessment to exclude sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or confluent rash with blistering or desquamation indicating severe cutaneous disease
High-volume diarrhoea with haemorrhage, severe pain, or ileus
Rising bilirubin indicating severe hepatic involvement
Superimposed opportunistic infection during intensified immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Lower-grade disease usually responds to corticosteroids with good outcomes, whereas high-grade or steroid-refractory disease carries substantial mortality driven both by the disease itself and by infection during intensified immunosuppression; acute graft-versus-host disease remains a leading cause of transplant-related morbidity and death.
pitfalls: Attributing diarrhoea or rash to graft-versus-host disease without excluding infection such as cytomegalovirus or Clostridioides difficile
Intensifying immunosuppression while missing a concurrent opportunistic infection
Under-recognising upper-gut disease presenting only as anorexia and nausea
Confusing conditioning-related mucositis or a drug rash with early disease
Overlooking sinusoidal obstruction syndrome as an alternative explanation for cholestasis
references: Consensus grading criteria for acute graft-versus-host disease
Standard haematopoietic cell transplantation reference texts
management: First-line systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay for grade II or higher disease
Continuation or optimisation of calcineurin-inhibitor prophylaxis with ciclosporin or tacrolimus
Ruxolitinib or extracorporeal photopheresis for steroid-refractory disease
Topical corticosteroids for cutaneous disease and non-absorbable enteral steroids such as budesonide for gut involvement
Supportive care with skin protection, fluid and electrolyte replacement for diarrhoea, and nutritional support
Antimicrobial and antifungal prophylaxis with surveillance for cytomegalovirus and other viral reactivation during intensified immunosuppression
Management within the specialist haematopoietic stem cell transplant team
